newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK'S JOCKEY CLUB VOWS RACE CLEAN-UP AFTER SCANDAL.
newsitem.headline: HK'S JOCKEY CLUB VOWS RACE CLEAN-UP AFTER SCANDAL.

text.p: Hong Kong's Jockey Club vowed on Tuesday to clean up the race tracks and punish any jockeys or trainers found guilty of race fixing in the territory's biggest horseracing scandal, in which 37 people have been detained.
The club, which has a monopoly on racing and race gaming in the British colony, said it would go ahead with weekend races despite the turmoil of the biggest race fixing inquiry in more than a decade.
The territory's anti-corruption police meanwhile said they had freed 19 detainees on bail, but the probe was widening.
"The Hong Kong Jockey Club is determined to keep horse racing clean," Wilson Cheng, the club's information secretary, told Reuters.
"Racing will continue as scheduled on Saturday," he said.

Cheng also said the club would not suspend any jockeys and trainers due to take part in this Saturday's race meeting unless they were actually incriminated by the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) investigation.
"After we hear more from the ICAC, our stewards will take appropriate actions," he said.
On Monday the ICAC said 37 people had been arrested, including five jockeys, two trainers and three Jockey Club staff.
On Tuesday 18 were still being questioned, the ICAC said.
So far nobody has been charged. The ICAC cannot hold the detainees longer than 48 hours without bringing charges.

The races are the only legal outlet for a flutter in gambling-mad Hong Kong. The horse track is one of the biggest businesses in the territory of 6.4 million people, outperforming some weighty blue chip companies in turnover.
Betting turnover in the 1995/96 season was HK$80 billion (US$11 billion), believed the highest per capita in the world.

The ICAC probe has become front page news and diverted the public eye away from the political polemics and Sino-British wrangling that has dominated the news this year as China prepares to take the territory back from Britain on July 1.
Editorialists and cartoonists had a field day. Many of them sang the praises of the ICAC and the Jockey Club for acting swiftly to protect fair racing.
"In the long run, the Jockey Club's determination to act will boost local and international confidence," the independent daily Ming Pao said.
A cartoon in the English-language South China Morning Post showed an ICAC troubleshooter wearing a gas mask entering the stables to eliminate a foul odour.
